opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, a lot of it came down to risk management. When you're building a flagship model under real time pressure, you want to stack as few unknowns on top of each other as possible. Gemini 1.0 was already doing a lot of new things at once: it was natively multimodal from the start, it was trained on TPU infrastructure at a scale we hadn't used before, and the data mixture was quite different. Each of those carries its own risk of training instabilities or surprises you only find out about weeks into a run.

Mixture-of-experts is something Google has a long history with. Going back to the sparsely-gated MoE work, then GShard, Switch Transformer and GLaM, we knew it could give you much better quality per unit of compute. But we also knew it's harder to get right at scale. You have to deal with load balancing across experts, routing instabilities, the communication cost of moving tokens between devices, and serving complexity, because the memory footprint is much larger than the active compute. None of that is unsolvable, but if something goes wrong in a giant run, it's much harder to work out whether the problem is the architecture, the multimodal data, or the infrastructure.

So the pragmatic choice was to ship a strong dense model first, get the multimodal recipe and the infrastructure solid, and learn from that. Once that foundation was in place, bringing MoE back in, which is what you saw with 1.5, was a much more contained change. And it paid off. Combined with the long-context work, it gave a big jump in efficiency and capability.

That's my perspective on it, anyway. Decisions like that involve a lot of people and trade-offs, but the general principle is that you don't want to change everything at once on your most important run.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I should say up front that I can only speak from what's been publicly shared and from my general understanding of how these large training efforts work, so take this as my read rather than any inside account.

The first thing to keep in mind is that Gemini 1.0 was a bit of a unification moment. You had the DeepMind side and the Google Brain side coming together, and the priority was shipping a strong, stable, natively multimodal model on a very aggressive timeline. When you're doing that, you tend to minimize the number of risky bets you stack on top of each other. Mixture-of-experts is a well-understood idea at Google, going all the way back to the Shazeer work and then GShard, Switch Transformer, GLaM, and so on. But "well-understood in research" and "de-risked at frontier scale, across text, image, audio, and video, with serving guarantees" are two different things.

Second, MoE really changes the systems problem. Dense models are comparatively simple to shard and to serve predictably. With experts, you have routing, load balancing, all-to-all communication across TPU pods, memory footprint that doesn't shrink even though compute per token does, and a whole set of latency and cost questions on the inference side. If your goal is to get something deployed into Bard, into Workspace, into Pixel, with tight quality and latency targets, dense buys you predictability.

Third, I think there's an evaluation and training stability dimension. Sparse models can be more finicky during training, and when you're also pushing on long context, multimodality, and a new post-training pipeline, you'd rather isolate variables. You want to be able to attribute a regression to one thing, not three.

So my interpretation is less that MoE was deferred for any lack of belief in it, and more that 1.0 was about establishing the baseline and the infrastructure. Once you have that foundation and the serving stack in place, MoE becomes the obvious next lever for scaling capability at manageable cost. And of course, that's essentially what you then saw with 1.5, where they talked openly about the sparse architecture and the long context work. In hindsight, it looks like sequencing, not a change of heart.

astra-6.text:
I don’t know the specific reasoning behind that decision, but mixture-of-experts models introduce a lot of engineering complexity. You activate only a subset of the model for each token, which can make computation more efficient, but you also have to get routing, load balancing, and communication between devices right. Those challenges affect both training stability and serving efficiency.

For a first release, the team may have prioritized getting the overall model working reliably before introducing that additional complexity. But I’d be careful about treating that as Google’s actual rationale—that’s a possible explanation, not something I can confirm.
